The predicate divergence of the fast-follow below, read in the source: routineWait is Armed or Merging or an Unmergeable whose Routine() is true, which ghautomerge.go:303 defines as BLOCKED or UNKNOWN only, while waitingOnGitHub admits every Unmergeable including BEHIND, DRAFT and DIRTY - the three states ghautomerge's own comment at :299-302 says wait on someone rather than on GitHub.

I read the required checks of the code commit on GitHub myself before approving and carry no verdict or run id forward as what the head holds now: the required set is lint, typecheck, test and pr-title with no branch-protection checks, every required name's newest run at the code commit had completed and succeeded when I read it, nothing there was failed, cancelled or timed out, the only lane still running was the non-required dispatch check, and the compare from that commit to the head I approve returned handoffsOnly true over two files.
consideredAndNotCarried: The code-quality half calls the notice's opening clause false for an Unmergeable, since choose sends no mutation in that state, so 'Legion submitted the merge ... and GitHub has not completed it' asserts an act that did not happen. I read it the other way and say why: the sentence summarises the row, which is a standing submission the daemon keeps making, and its two following clauses - that nothing has been withdrawn and that the daemon goes on submitting it - are exactly true of an Unmergeable. The cause it then quotes, 'the daemon merges it once GitHub reports it mergeable', agrees rather than contradicts, which is what separates this from the Lagging and Disappeared cases I did block on, where the quoted cause said the pull request was closed or the arm was gone. Round thirteen's deep-review half reached the same reading independently and called it within tolerance.

The same half's reading that waitingOnGitHub should be routineWait, third time this design has been raised. The new fact it brings is the divergence, which I verified and carry to the fast-follow line with the sentence that should be written; the choice between one predicate and two is the architect's and is not a correctness risk. Telling the architect about a BEHIND or a DRAFT is arguably better than routineWait's classification would give, since those are the waits a person must end; what is missing is any sentence saying the two predicates differ and why.

fastFollow: waitingOnGitHub and routineWait classify the same ghautomerge types in one package and disagree by one term - every Unmergeable against an Unmergeable whose Routine() is true - with neither doc naming the other. Whichever way it is settled, one sentence on each predicate naming the other and the term of difference is the minimum, and expressing the wider set in ghautomerge where the states live would leave a wait type added later classified once rather than twice.

The merge-waiting remedy enumeration omits the Unmergeable states a person must end - a branch GitHub requires to be up to date with its base, a draft, a conflict - in the notice's own reason and in five mirrors. This is the second round it has been named and it is now sharper: those are precisely the states waitingOnGitHub admits and routineWait does not.
A content edit made inside a forward-merge commit is invisible to a parent-against-parent read; this one was right and disclosed, but the practice is worth a line in the conflicts reference.
